phases.title: Mong Mao → Upper Myanmar → Patkai
phases.text: Sukaphaa’s party departed in the conventional 1215 chronology and reached Assam in 1228, after thirteen years of movement and stays. The gold line progressively reveals that journey. The moving party symbol uses illustrative pacing; intermediate annual positions and arrival dates at Myanmar stops are unknown. Unreached reference places stay hidden.

phases.title: Across the Patkai to Namrup
phases.text: Sukaphaa entered the Assam plains by an overland Patkai crossing. Pangsau is the conventional pass identification; the line shown is an approximate corridor. Namrup is the first Assam stop in this sequence. This is a migrating group, not yet the later Ahom kingdom.

phases.title: Dihing exploration and Tipam
phases.text: The chronicle sequence crosses the Sessa, goes upstream on the Dihing, then returns downstream to Tipam. Exact camps and the riverbank track cannot be recovered. The river excursion is schematic; no upstream camp is plotted as an exact site.

phases.title: Mungklang / Abhaypur
phases.text: Sukaphaa moved from Tipam to Mungklang Chekhru, identified in histories as Abhaypur. Its exact historical site is unresolved here, so it is listed without a false map pin. Earlier locality patches stand for the settlement network, not continuous possession.

phases.title: Habung: cultivation and floods
phases.text: The chronicles place a move down the Brahmaputra to Habung in 1240. Flooding prompted another move in 1244. The pin uses the modern Dhakuakhana-area identification; the historical tract was broader and is also associated with the Dhemaji region.

phases.title: Downstream to Dikhoumukh, then Ligirigaon
phases.text: From Habung the party followed the Brahmaputra downstream to the Dikhou mouth and travelled up the Dikhou toward Ligirigaon (Song-Tak), near present Nazira. Changing channels and uncertain old settlements make the trail a corridor rather than a literal boat track.

phases.title: Simaluguri settlement
phases.text: Simaluguri became the next base, with a detachment left at Ligirigaon. The historical settlement is associated with the modern Simaluguri vicinity; the marker is approximate. These are local footholds, not a continuous kingdom stretching to Sadiya.

phases.title: Charaideo: capital and a small kingdom
phases.text: Charaideo became the enduring capital in 1253 in the conventional chronology; some histories give 1251–1252. The surrounding foothill-and-plain core grew through coercion, accommodation and marriage with Moran and Barahi groups. The reconstructed core remains much smaller than the 16th-century realm.

phases.title: Toward the Dikhou–Namdang tract
phases.text: Suteuphaa’s reign is associated with gaining land from the Kacharis in the Dikhou–Namdang tract. The exact acquisition year is unknown: 1268 starts the display window, not a dated conquest. This small western addition precedes a long period of consolidation. The adopted river-frontier display uses Dikhou and Dehing for the core, replacing the earlier hand-drawn outline; it does not map an additional west-of-Dikhou claim.

phases.title: Consolidation, not continuous expansion
phases.text: The kingdom largely held its Upper Assam core for roughly two centuries. Campaigns, a Kamata conflict and eastern diplomacy do not establish permanent annexation of the routes traversed. Sudangphaa’s Patkai settlement belongs to frontier consolidation, not an automatic conquest of all intervening hills.

phases.title: Suhungmung: preparations for expansion
phases.text: Suhungmung’s reign brought administrative reorganisation, a population enquiry in 1510 and campaigns against neighbouring groups. The map retains the inherited core until specific territorial acquisitions are reported.

phases.title: Habung annexed
phases.text: Habung was annexed under Suhungmung. A separate north-bank patch marks this gain; it does not yet colour the whole Chutia kingdom as Ahom.

phases.title: Dikhoumukh fighting and eastern gains
phases.text: A Chutia offensive was defeated at Dikhoumukh and on the river. Ahom gains around Mungkhrang and a Namdang locality followed. This eastern Namdang must not be confused automatically with the Sivasagar tributary of that name; the eastern patch is a broad Dihing-area locator, not an exact fort.

phases.title: Chutia counterattack: eastern setback
phases.text: The Chutias retook Mungkhrang and the associated eastern tract after the Ahom garrison withdrew. The eastern Ahom patch disappears and a contested Chutia recovery patch returns. Sources do not securely establish the extent of any Habung recovery, so the north-bank ownership is shown as unresolved during this interval.

phases.title: Ahom recovery and advance
phases.text: Suhungmung recovered the lost eastern tract and established a fort farther east in the river-mouth zone. The source names Sessa and Tiphao; modern identifications vary. The expansion is schematic and is not labelled as a securely located fort.

phases.title: Sadiya and the Chutia kingdom annexed
phases.text: The decisive campaigns ended the independent Chutia monarchy in 1523–1524. Sadiya came under an Ahom governor, the Sadiya Khowa Gohain. The eastern domain now joins the older core; this does not yet imply the later western extent toward the Kolong. The Kachari frontier does not automatically retreat with this separate Chutia conquest. From 1526 the Dhansiri campaign corridor is shown as hatching, reflecting clashes before the approximate 1532 settled-map stage.

phases.title: Westward campaigns against the Kacharis
phases.text: The 1526 campaign and renewed 1531 Marangi fighting preceded this approximate 1532 settled-border stage. The map no longer retreats the Kachari boundary in 1523. Dimapur was sacked in 1536; the later Kolong-side phase begins in 1537.

phases.date: Before the late 14th century · founding date uncertain
phases.title: Sadiya centre; early extent unknown
phases.text: 1187 and Birpal belong to a later founding tradition, not a securely dated conquest sequence. Only a small symbolic Sadiya-area patch is shown in this early window. It neither measures the early state nor assigns the later Lakhimpur–Dhemaji domain to it.

phases.title: Chutia power becomes clearer in the records
phases.text: Chronicles place conflict with the Ahoms in Sutuphaa’s time, conventionally around 1376. Nandin / Nandisvara is the earliest king remembered in the inscription genealogy of Satyanarayana. This supports an eastern political centre, not a precise founding year or frontier.

phases.title: Dhenukhana grant: western evidence appears
phases.text: The grant of Satyanarayana and Pratyakshanarayana provides dated evidence in the Habung–Dhakuakhana region. An additional locality patch marks this evidence. Its appearance in 1392 is an attestation date, not proof that the tract was conquered that year.

phases.title: Ghilamara: Lakshminarayana’s grant
phases.text: Lakshminarayana’s Ghilamara charter adds another dated western record. Its locality patch joins the earlier Sadiya and Habung-region symbols. The map does not fill the intervening country from this grant alone or assign a conquest to 1401.

phases.title: Sadiya–Chepakhowa charter and Habung
phases.text: Durlabhnarayana’s charter names a Habung authority. Genealogical references to a Kamatapura ruler have competing interpretations and do not justify colouring all Kamata as Chutia territory. The Habung and Sadiya markers locate regions, not the charter’s exact original issue/find sites.

phases.title: Tamreswari: an eastern royal inscription
phases.text: The Paya–Tamreswari inscription records Mukta-dharmanarayana’s temple enclosure wall in 1442. Alongside the earlier grants, this supports a mid-15th-century domain context in the eastern plains and river valleys. The wider envelope is reconstructed, not a conquest in 1442; upland Arunachal is not automatically annexed.

phases.title: Habung lost; Ahom–Chutia war
phases.text: Ahom annexation of Habung was followed by Chutia offensives and reverses in the Dihing–Dikhoumukh theatre. The Habung patch changes owner separately from the Sadiya heartland. Dhirnarayana’s exact accession is unknown, and royal names vary between chronicles.

phases.title: Mungkhrang recovered
phases.text: A Chutia counterattack recovered the eastern tract around Mungkhrang. The map restores a symbolic recovery patch there. Claims of a simultaneous, complete reconquest of Habung are less secure and are not treated as a settled border change.

phases.title: Ahom counteroffensive
phases.text: The Ahoms recovered their eastern losses and advanced toward the river mouths. Chutia control contracted toward Sadiya before the final campaign. A land grant or findspot by itself cannot define every wartime frontier.

phases.title: Independent monarchy ends; people and traditions continue
phases.text: Ahom annexation ended independent Chutia kingship around 1523–1524. Chronicles disagree over the last royal names and deaths. Chutia communities, specialists and Deori religious traditions continued; a polity’s disappearance from the map does not mean its population disappeared.

phases.title: Sandhya’s western reorganisation
phases.text: The map begins with a Kamatapur–western plains focus and an uncertain successor region farther east. This is a change of political centre, not a newly conquered kingdom growing from zero. The capital-shift date and frontier are approximate.

phases.title: Rival rulers and competing authority
phases.text: Durlabhnarayana and Indranarayana belong to approximate 14th-century chronologies. Kamata authority was contested; the eastern reach is dashed and separate from the western core. No automatic, continuous rule to the later Barnadi limit is assumed.

phases.title: Fragmentation before the Khen
phases.text: Arimatta and successor traditions cannot furnish exact borders or reigns. The reconstruction contracts to the western Kamata focus, while independent Bhuyan localities remain distinct. The c.1365 division is a display anchor, not a securely dated territorial collapse.

phases.title: Niladhwaj: Kamatapur base
phases.text: A western core represents the early Khen kingdom. The c.1440 foundation is conventional; the later Nilambar footprint is not shown at the dynasty’s beginning.

phases.title: Chakradhwaj: consolidation
phases.text: An intermediate western-plains envelope locates the kingdom during consolidation. The larger outline is a schematic stage, not a dated annexation of each district.

phases.title: Nilambar: wider Kamata domain
phases.text: Nilambar’s later kingdom reached farther into lower Assam; a broad reconstruction extends toward the Barnadi area. The transition at 1480 follows approximate reign chronology. Husain Shah captured Kamatapur in 1498.

phases.title: Regional chiefs, not a single Bhuyan kingdom
phases.text: Bhuyan is a category of landed chiefs, not one dynasty or a permanently united set of twelve. Separate Bharali–Borgang and Buroi–Dikrong river sectors show the adopted central-valley setting. Dates, membership and boundaries are uncertain; this early interval does not establish the later Chandivara lineage at these precise sites. River-bounded sectors are an adopted approximate reconstruction, not mapped estates of specific chiefs. The Barnadi side uses the existing qualified Puthimari/Bornadi reference trace.

phases.title: Chandivara and the Barnadi region
phases.text: Charit traditions associate Chandivara’s group with Langamaguri / Lengamaguri near the Barnadi. Exact date and site are unresolved. A Barnadi–north Dhansiri river sector replaces the round locator; separate Bharali–Borgang and Buroi–Dikrong sectors remain. River-bounded sectors are an adopted approximate reconstruction, not mapped estates of specific chiefs. The Barnadi side uses the existing qualified Puthimari/Bornadi reference trace.

phases.title: Bardowa: the Shiromani Bhuyan lineage
phases.text: Sankardeva was born into a Bhuyan family at Bardowa in 1449. This adds a securely associated south-bank centre; it is not the year the Bhuyans conquered Bardowa. The whole Kolong–Brahmaputra sector represents the associated south-bank region, alongside separate north-bank river sectors. River-bounded sectors are an adopted approximate reconstruction, not mapped estates of specific chiefs. The Barnadi side uses the existing qualified Puthimari/Bornadi reference trace.

phases.title: Sultanate pressure and local resistance
phases.text: The Bengal conquest displaced the Khen monarchy. The extent and duration of the garrisons varied; local chiefs remained important. The western resistance stage is separated from the older central-valley seats. River-bounded sectors are an adopted approximate reconstruction, not mapped estates of specific chiefs. The Barnadi side uses the existing qualified Puthimari/Bornadi reference trace.

phases.title: Local recovery after Bengal’s withdrawal
phases.text: Independent chiefs re-emerged after the Bengal garrisons lost control. The c.1505 change is an approximate display anchor, not proof of a single Harupnarayan state extending from Sankosh to Subansiri. River-bounded sectors are an adopted approximate reconstruction, not mapped estates of specific chiefs. The Barnadi side uses the existing qualified Puthimari/Bornadi reference trace.

phases.title: Koch advance in the west; Ahom pressure in the east
phases.text: Biswa Singha subdued western chiefs over a sequence of campaigns, while Ahom expansion reduced eastern autonomy. The river sectors contract in stages; neither all chiefs nor both banks fell in one year. River-bounded sectors are an adopted approximate reconstruction, not mapped estates of specific chiefs. The Barnadi side uses the existing qualified Puthimari/Bornadi reference trace.

phases.title: Chiefly independence declines; offices persist
phases.text: Regional Bhuyan seats were progressively subordinated by larger states. This map ends the independent-chiefdom layer in the 1530s, not every Bhuyan family or office. Local and district histories also record later Bhuyan authority and resistance. River-bounded sectors are an adopted approximate reconstruction, not mapped estates of specific chiefs. The Barnadi side uses the existing qualified Puthimari/Bornadi reference trace.

phases.title: Chikna: a small foothill beginning
phases.text: The initial map shows a small regional foothill base. An exact founding border is unknown. Intermediate outlines and early stage years are approximate reconstructions.

phases.title: Consolidating neighbouring chiefdoms
phases.text: Nearby-chief campaigns are represented by an approximate plains enlargement. This date is an editorial anchor. Intermediate outlines and early stage years are approximate reconstructions.

phases.title: Western Kamata and the Duars
phases.text: The western envelope expands. Capitals are associated with movement toward the plains, but transfer dates are unresolved. Intermediate outlines and early stage years are approximate reconstructions.

phases.title: Biswa Singha’s later domain
phases.text: The later reign uses a mature western domain. Ahom contact after the Turbak war is distinct from early founding. Intermediate outlines and early stage years are approximate reconstructions.

phases.title: Naranarayan inherits the core
phases.text: Accession inherits the core; it does not create the later eastern conquests. Intermediate outlines and early stage years are approximate reconstructions.

phases.title: First eastern advance, then Pichala
phases.text: An eastern campaigning zone appears separately from the western core. Intermediate outlines and early stage years are approximate reconstructions.

phases.title: Withdrawal and preparation
phases.text: The eastern campaign fails; the map removes its hatching after Pichala rather than retaining the advance as permanent rule. Intermediate outlines and early stage years are approximate reconstructions.

phases.title: Chilarai’s renewed eastern campaign
phases.text: Chilarai renews the eastern invasion. Wartime hatching is distinct from core territory. Intermediate outlines and early stage years are approximate reconstructions.

phases.title: Majuli settlement and contested overlordship
phases.text: Koch forces reached Majuli and occupied Garhgaon. For the 1563–1580 settlement phase, north-bank land west of the Subansiri is shown as Koch and land east as Ahom. Both sides follow the same river trace. The 1581 successor-state geography is separate. The campaign markers do not imply permanent annexation of Majuli or the whole Ahom kingdom.

phases.title: Rajmahal: formal conquest, incomplete control
phases.text: Western provincial context appears; the eastern chiefs and coast remain outside settled imperial control. Intermediate region outlines are approximate modern geographic proxies.

phases.title: Rebellion and uneven western control
phases.text: Hatching marks contested authority. The regional envelope is not a recovered annual frontier. Intermediate region outlines are approximate modern geographic proxies.

phases.title: Western consolidation; eastern resistance persists
phases.text: The eastern regional resistance layer remains distinct. Intermediate region outlines are approximate modern geographic proxies.

phases.title: Eastern campaign and the Dhaka base
phases.text: Advance is hatched; Dhaka becomes the provincial base in 1610. Intermediate region outlines are approximate modern geographic proxies.

phases.title: Bhati and delta submissions
phases.text: The delta stage expands while Sylhet’s Afghan resistance remains separate. Intermediate region outlines are approximate modern geographic proxies.

phases.title: Sylhet consolidation; western Koch Hajo invasion
phases.text: The Bengal stage expands; a hatched western-Assam sector represents the opening of the 1612–1613 campaign. Intermediate region outlines are approximate modern geographic proxies.

phases.title: Koch Hajo annexed; Kamrup administration
phases.text: The Koch Hajo core passes to Mughal administration. Intermediate region outlines are approximate modern geographic proxies.

phases.title: Kamrup resistance and reconsolidation
phases.text: Post-conquest hatching marks resistance, not a restored unified kingdom. Intermediate region outlines are approximate modern geographic proxies.

phases.title: Eastern invasion checked by the Ahoms
phases.text: Eastward reach is temporary; the next stage removes it. Darrang’s Ahom-protected succession differs from annexed western Kamrup. Intermediate region outlines are approximate modern geographic proxies.

phases.title: Bengal and Kamrup; Chittagong still outside
phases.text: The eastern coastal addition has not yet occurred. Later Assam wars remain separately dated on the map. Intermediate region outlines are approximate modern geographic proxies.

phases.title: Chittagong joins Mughal Bengal
phases.text: The coastal proxy is added; hill tracts and northern principalities are excluded from direct-rule shading. Intermediate region outlines are approximate modern geographic proxies.

phases.title: Bengal’s autonomous nawabs
phases.text: Nominal Mughal sovereignty differs from direct control from Delhi. The Diwani transition follows in 1765. Intermediate region outlines are approximate modern geographic proxies.

phases.title: Koch Hajo: the Assam core
phases.text: Core and eastern dependencies are distinguished; the modern Bangladesh extension is removed.

phases.title: Pressure from Mughal Bengal
phases.text: Koch Bihar’s submission does not automatically annex Koch Hajo. Parikshit continues to resist.

phases.title: Western invasion during the 1612–1613 campaign
phases.text: The Dhubri-side campaign overlay shows advance before the annexation stage; no precise monthly frontier is invented.

phases.title: Kolong-side inherited frontier
phases.text: This is the inherited reconstruction before the Koch war; the 1537 phase is a display convention following the 1536 campaigns.

phases.title: Majuli settlement: Subansiri frontier
phases.text: The treaty’s north-bank cession does not permanently annex Majuli or the Ahom capital to Koch territory.

phases.title: Before the Barnadi transition
phases.text: The inherited frontier is distinct from later Ahom presence and tributary reach farther west.

phases.title: Koch Hajo collapse and frontier contact
phases.text: Political or military reach is shown separately from annexed core. The first round of war spans 1615–1616.

phases.title: Samdhara and tributary Darrang
phases.text: Balinarayan/Dharmanarayan’s dependent Darrang layer carries Ahom political reach westward. It is not immediate direct annexation of all Kamrup.

phases.title: Pandu captured; Hajo attack fails
phases.text: Gait records November 1617 capture and fortification of Pandu, then a failed Hajo assault and retreat. This is an early Guwahati-region military milestone, not continuous whole-city annexation.
phases.southBank: Pandu advance from the Kajali-side base

phases.title: Frontier warfare and dependent chiefs
phases.text: Temporary operations and local submissions do not establish one continuously administered western province.

phases.title: Hajo and wider western successes
phases.text: The reach layer records the broad advance; the subsequent Mughal counter-offensive prevents treating it as permanent annexation.

phases.title: Mughal counter-offensive and Ahom reverses
phases.text: Exact positions changed during the 1637–1639 war. The annual rearward envelope is explicitly schematic; the next treaty is a separate event.

phases.title: Asurar Ali: two different bank boundaries
phases.text: The 1639 terms must not be represented by one longitude through Kajali or Hajo. River and post alignments use modern reference geometry.

phases.title: Guwahati and Lower Assam expansion
phases.text: The capture/consolidation window is 1658–1660: Gait places the advance in the 1658 succession context, while other accounts give Guwahati in 1659 and wider Kamrup in 1660. The map adopts 1658 as a qualified annual anchor.
phases.northBank: Manas core; farther-west reach to Sankosh

phases.title: Mir Jumla occupies Guwahati and Garhgaon
phases.text: Occupied Kamrup and the farther-eastern invasion are distinguished. The occupation of the capital is not a new permanent Mughal frontier.

phases.title: Ghilajharighat retreat
phases.text: The reduced bank-specific position precedes Lachit’s recovery in 1667.

phases.title: Lachit recovers Guwahati; Saraighat defends it
phases.text: The recovery appears in 1667 itself. Saraighat in 1671 is a defence of the recovered position, not the first capture of Guwahati.

phases.title: Guwahati surrendered again
phases.text: The exact frontier beyond the documented forts is unresolved. The shape is a qualified rearward envelope, not a surveyed boundary.

phases.title: Final recovery and lasting Manas frontier
phases.text: Gadadhar Singha’s final recovery in 1682 fixes the durable western frontier. This is separate from the earlier 1667 recovery.

spots.name: Mong Mao ≈ · 1215
spots.note: Regional locator near modern Ruili / the Shweli valley, western Yunnan. Not an exact palace or departure point. Some chronicle traditions instead associate departure with Mong Mit in 1227.

spots.name: Waingmaw / Myitkyina ≈
spots.note: Modern regional reference for the Wieng Maw identification and upper Irrawaddy crossing in the Comprehensive History account. Crossing point and stop date uncertain.

spots.name: Mogaung / Mong Kwang ≈
spots.note: Mong Kwang/Mogaung is named in migration accounts. Modern town used to locate the region; no year or exact medieval camp assigned.

spots.name: Hukawng valley ≈ · Myanmar
spots.note: Broad valley locator within the documented regional corridor; the winding line does not trace a particular historic road.

spots.name: Nong Yang / Khamjang ≈
spots.date: Near the end of the 1215–1228 journey
spots.note: Traditional lake/Khamjang association near Pangsau. Uses the modern Nong Yang lake identification; historical camp perimeter and date remain uncertain.

spots.name: Pangsau / Patkai · 1228 ≈
spots.note: Approximate overland crossing corridor; exact medieval track unverified.

spots.name: Namrup · 1228
spots.note: Modern locality used for the arrival-region marker.

spots.name: Tipam · c.1230
spots.note: Locality identification approximate; the upstream Dihing camp is not exactly located.

spots.name: Habung · 1240
spots.note: Dhakuakhana-area identification; wider historical tract and settlement site uncertain.

spots.name: Dikhou mouth · 1244
spots.note: River-mouth corridor; modern course is not the medieval channel.

spots.name: Ligirigaon ≈ · 1244
spots.note: Nazira vicinity, not an excavated or fixed historical camp.

spots.name: Simaluguri ≈ · 1246
spots.note: Modern vicinity; historical site and river channels uncertain.

spots.name: Charaideo · 1253
spots.note: First enduring capital; modern archaeological location.

spots.name: Dikhou–Namdang tract ≈
spots.note: Regional locator; exact acquisition year unknown.

spots.name: Habung · 1512
spots.note: Symbolic regional patch, separate from Sadiya.

spots.name: Habung · control uncertain
spots.note: Wartime ownership is not securely fixed for the whole tract.

spots.name: Sadhayapura / Sadiya ≈
spots.date: Early foundation unknown; inscriptions late 14th century onward
spots.note: Regional centre; the precise medieval capital footprint is not fixed.

spots.name: Dhenukhana / Habung ≈
spots.note: Regional locator, not an exact charter findspot.

spots.name: Ghilamara · 1401
spots.note: Modern vicinity; land grant attests authority, not an acquisition date.

spots.name: Tamreswari / Paya ≈
spots.note: Temple region east of Sadiya; approximate point.

spots.name: Kamatapur / Gosanimari
spots.note: Gosanimari ruins locate Kamatapur; exact shift date disputed.

spots.name: Kamatapur / Gosanimari
spots.note: Fortified capital; staged envelopes are reconstructed.

spots.name: Langamaguri / Barnadi region ≈
spots.note: Exact settlement not fixed; broad regional locator.

spots.name: Bardowa / Batadrava
spots.note: A Bhuyan lineage centre, not a newly conquered province.

spots.name: North-bank chiefdoms ≈
spots.note: Symbolic regional locator; not one capital or fixed confederacy.

spots.name: Majuli · Koch camp (1563)
spots.note: Naranarayan camped at Majuli during the campaign. The pin is a present-day island reference, not a verified camp site or proof of permanent island annexation.

spots.name: Garhgaon · occupied (1563)
spots.note: Koch forces occupied the Ahom capital; occupation and Ahom tribute are not equivalent to permanent annexation. The marker uses the existing approximate capital reference.

spots.name: Dhubri · siege
spots.date: 1612–1613 campaign; sources differ on annual dating
spots.note: Western fortress/siege stage before the advance into Kamrup. Modern town reference, not a surveyed camp.

spots.name: Hajo · annexed Kamrup
spots.note: Regional administrative reference, not a claim that all resistance ended in 1613.

spots.name: Dhaka · base from 1610
spots.note: Modern city reference.

spots.name: Chittagong · 1666
spots.note: Coastal conquest, not blanket direct annexation of the Chittagong Hill Tracts.

spots.name: Samdhara · 1616
spots.note: Modern regional fort/confluence reference; the victory is followed by tributary Darrang.

spots.name: Pandu · temporary capture
spots.note: Temporary capture and fortification before the failed Hajo assault. This does not establish permanent whole-city annexation.

spots.name: Hajo · western campaign
spots.note: Temporary western success followed by Mughal counter-offensive.

spots.name: Guwahati · 1658–1660 window
spots.note: Capture and wider consolidation are differently dated. Modern city reference; historical river channels and town banks differed.

spots.name: Guwahati · occupied 1662
spots.note: Mir Jumla occupies Guwahati before advancing to Garhgaon.

spots.name: Guwahati · recovered 1667
spots.note: Lachit’s recovery precedes Saraighat. This is not the first Ahom military presence in the Guwahati region.

spots.name: Guwahati · surrendered 1679
spots.note: Mughal possession resumes during internal Ahom instability.

spots.name: Guwahati · final recovery 1682
spots.note: Gadadhar Singha restores control; the lasting Manas frontier follows.

routes.note: 1215–1228 migration corridor: Mong Mao region → upper Irrawaddy/Waingmaw–Myitkyina vicinity → Mogaung → Hukawng → Nong Yang → Patkai/Pangsau. Only the travelled fraction is revealed from 1215 to 1228. Annual positions interpolate distance for playback; they are not documented stop dates. Winding bends are illustrative, not a surveyed track or proof of specific camps. Alternative source itineraries exist.

progress.note: Illustrative pacing over thirteen years; intermediate annual positions are not historically dated.

routes.note: 1228 overland Patkai–Namrup corridor; Pangsau identification conventional, exact path unknown.

Reported upstream Dihing exploration and return to Tipam; line follows the modern river approximately, not a GPS trail. Drawn river sections share every vertex with the river layer. Gaps indicate unresolved historic access/confluences; no straight bridge is invented.

Sequence toward Habung via the Brahmaputra. Intermediate Mungklang/Abhaypur site is unresolved and intentionally not pinned; historical channels differed. The short cross-channel/access links are schematic land/access connectors; the river sections reuse the base map vertices. Drawn river sections share every vertex with the river layer. Gaps indicate unresolved historic access/confluences; no straight bridge is invented.

1244: Habung down the Brahmaputra to Dikhoumukh, then upriver toward Ligirigaon; schematic river corridor. Drawn river sections share every vertex with the river layer. Gaps indicate unresolved historic access/confluences; no straight bridge is invented.
1246 locality connection; exact camp and track unknown.
1253 conventional capital establishment: approximate overland connection to Charaideo.
